english: When it arises in men who wish for harm,
why: The anger arises in oneself, and it is the ill-wishers who rejoice when it does; it does not arise in them.

english: regarding the meaning of reality which possesses equanimity [note: original: "upeksha"], characterized as being free from definitions: those who are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones,
why: 'Indifferent to the object of reality' qualifies the Buddhas, who treat the reality-object (free of characteristics) with indifference; reality does not 'possess equanimity'.

english: It should be understood how these are produced.
why: This finishes the previous side's sentence: the neutral (avyākṛta) items should be understood to produce a cause-concordant result, not 'how these are produced'.

english: Therefore, these are held to be the objects of the mind.
why: The words are held to have the mental (conceptual) object as their domain; they are not themselves objects of mind.

english: An example of this is the relationship of smoke to fire.
why: The example is fire in relation to smoke: fire causes smoke but not its diminution.

english: makes the Primary Matrix (pradhāna) primordial matter entirely hollow and devoid of intrinsic nature
why: In the quoted verse it is what comes into the range of sight that is utterly hollow and without essence; the Tibetan does not say it 'makes' the pradhāna hollow.

english: The engagement of the mind apprehending an entity produces an incompatible cause in the form of a latent impression, which the mind apprehending a non-entity then interrupts.
why: It is the cognition of non-entity that, by producing an incompatible cause in the form of a latent impression, cuts off the continuum of the operating cognition of an entity; the English makes the entity-cognition produce its own incompatible cause.

english: but they do not cease to belong to the category of reasons in that sense
why: The point is that deviant similarity and dissimilarity statements do not come to count as reasons, since the general rule has no scope in the exception's domain; the English implies they remain reasons.

english: the prince, together with the chief ministers, approached the lord of beings.
why: The subjects (སྐྱེ་རྒུ, prajāḥ), together with the prince and chief ministers, went to their lord; the people as agents are dropped.

english:
If one is free of that heart-tormenting anger
which is like a blazing, scorching fire,
yet abandons it, ill repute will befall him,
why: The stanza contrasts with the next one: ill repute befalls one who does NOT abandon the heart-tormenting anger; the English makes abandoning anger bring ill repute.

english:
the text now explains the duties of one who is under dependence:

"Even so, except for asking questions, these actions should be done for him," which means that the resident pupil should not only ask questions, but should also take charge
why: gnas here is the master who grants dependence: the passage gives the master's duties, who likewise does these things for the pupil, except that he need not ask permission.

english: are in no way existent entities, because they are not observed in any way whatsoever
why: ཇི་ལྟར་ཡང་ (kathaṃcit) means 'in some respect': the self, pot etc. are in some respect non-existent in nature because in some respect not observed, not 'in no way existent'.

english: At that time, you will remember me, who am free from worldly existence.
why: The ascetic's son asks to be remembered then for (his) freedom from existence; he is not already free, as the frame (he later attains arhatship from the Buddha) shows.

english: Indeed, a noble birth prevents one from falling into utter insignificance.
why: The verse argues that birth does not secure worth (men of great lineage are seen to be like dogs); the English asserts the opposite, contradicting its own next sentence.

english: This very nature of its co-present cooperative conditions, which is momentary
why: It is the thing's own momentary nature that is together with its cooperating factors, not the nature of the conditions.

english: In this way he has taught the cause of those who cling.
why: With honorific mnga' ba the clinging is the Buddha's (apparent) adherence: this shows the reason why he seems to have attachment, not the cause of others' clinging.

english: Remoteness in the case of inference is merely the opposite of subtlety of nature.
why: The Tibetan says NON-remoteness (མ་བསྐལ་བ) for inference is merely the opposite of subtle nature.

english: "You and the cowherd will come to know it through Śiva
why: The phrase concerns the cowherd's woman (མ) named Śivā, whose hand throws the curd pot; it is not the god Śiva and 'the cowherd' is not a separate party here.

english: because what does not remain to destroy it itself remains
why: If perishing depends on another, a cause of remaining is pointless because, as long as the destroyer is absent, the thing remains of itself.

english: yet that is a quality of the sapphire alone
why: The verse argues virtue is not from birth: even when a glass bead takes on the sapphire's colour, that is its (the bead's) own quality; 'of the sapphire alone' inverts the point.
